Software Required: QGIS LTR 3.44

## Overview

This exercise is the third hands-on block of the Week 1 GIS workshop, following directly on from [Part 2 – Raster Import](import-raster.qmd). You will work with RUDIFUN data of Vlissingen, inspect its values, create a choroplet map of densities.

**Learning Outcomes** #update

By completing this exercise, you will be able to:

✅ Import a raster layer into QGIS from the Browser Panel\
✅ Read raster statistics (min/max) and interpret a histogram\
✅ Style a raster using a pseudocolor ramp\
✅ Derive a binary risk-zone raster using a threshold expression\
✅ Export a raster layer and share a basemap screenshot

------------------------------------------------------------------------

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="true"}
**Background:** Met de RUDIFUN-dataset kunnen overheden, ruimtelijk onderzoekers, planologen en stedenbouwkundigen aan de slag voor onderzoek naar de samenhang tussen ruimtelijke dichtheden en menging van wonen met andere functies enerzijds en stedelijke dossiers als mobiliteit, leefbaarheid en vastgoedmarkt anderzijds.De Ruimtelijke Dichtheden en Functiemenging in Nederland (RUDIFUN) dataset geeft een indicatie van de dichtheid en morfologie van bebouwd gebied. Het geeft deze weer in onder andere de eenheden Floor-Space Index (FSI) en de Mixed Use Index (MXI). Deze eenheden zijn berekend op de schaal van bouwblok, buurt, wijk en gemeente. De kaart met de FSI geeft een indicatie van de ruimtelijke dichtheid van bebouwing. De MXI drukt de verhouding uit tussen wonen en werken. In de publicatie zijn de verschillende indexen en hun toepassingsmogelijkheden beschreven.Data aangeboden op dit portaal zijn te gebruiken onder voorwaarde van bronvermelding CC BY 4.0 NL.
:::

Students open the qgis project. it visualizes the whole RUDIFUN dataset for the Zeeland province. The layer is PV29\_\_00_Basis_Bouwblok

# data preparation

They open the attribute table They select the features belonging to the city of Vlissingen.

Select by expression: GM_CODE = GM0718

They save the selection as a new layer

Export \> Save selected Features as

Callout: why it is important to work with subsets? - more agile layers - less noise - focused analysis

Delete fields

keep only metrics related to 2024 and 2019. we will work only with FSI for this exercise

# first question: where are the densiest buurten in 2024?

- right click on the saved layer
- properties \> sympology
- select FSI_2024 for value
- select natural breaks (jenks)

answer: which areas are the most dense?

# second question: how densities changed?

- create a copy of the layer
- rename it as difference
- create a filter, excluding the areas with 0 FSI
  - right click \> properties \> source
  - in the provider specific expression box type the formula: "FSI_24"\>0
  - click ok

# Create the maps

Step 5: Create Cartographic Visualizations

5.1 Create a Classified Choropleth Map

A choropleth map uses colour gradients to display the spatial distribution of a continuous variable. Classifying continuous density data into discrete categories (e.g., 5 classes) makes the map easier to interpret and print.

Select the Data Layer:

In the Layers Panel, click on the layer containing the styled FSI

This layer should be visible on the map canvas

Open the Layer Styling Panel:

Go to View → Panels → Layer Styling (or press F7)

The Layer Styling panel opens on the right side

Change Classification Type to Graduated:

In the Symbology tab, locate the classification dropdown (top of the panel)

Click it and select Graduated

The panel will reconfigure to show classification options

Configure Classification Parameters:

Value (Column):

Click the dropdown below "Graduated"

Select FSI\_-\_2024

Classification Mode:

Click the dropdown labeled "Classification Mode" or "Method"

Select Quantiles (Equal Count)

This divides the data into classes such that each class contains approximately the same number of municipalities

Makes spatial patterns easier to see than equal-interval classification

Number of Classes:

Set to 5 (a standard choice balancing detail with simplicity)

tip: You can experiment with 4–7 depending on your data and preferences

tip: other classification methods

Choose a Colour Ramp:

Click the Color Ramp dropdown

Choose a sequential or diverging ramp suitable for FSI visualization

Blues, Greens, Purples – Single-hue sequential schemes

Reverse (optional): If you want low values in darker colours and high values in lighter colours, click the Reverse checkbox

Generate Classification Classes:

Click the Classify button

The tool automatically calculates class breaks based on your selected method

Class ranges will appear in a table below

Review the generated classes:

Each row shows a class range and its colour

Check that classes are logical and well-distributed

(Optional) Manually Edit Class Breaks:

Double-click any value in the "Value" or "Label" columns to edit it

Useful for rounding numbers or creating custom labels (e.g., "Low," "Medium," "High")

Adjust Styling Details:

Stroke (Outline):

Find "Stroke width" or similar option

Set to 0.5 pt (thin, subtle boundaries between meighborhoods)

This maintains visual distinction without overwhelming the map

Stroke color:

Choose a dark grey or black for contrast against the fill colours

Opacity:

Set to 90% to ensure clear visibility while subtly revealing underlying features

Apply and Review:

Click Apply to update the map canvas

Return to the main QGIS canvas and inspect the choropleth:

Southern municipalities should appear warmer (higher PV potential)

Northern municipalities should appear cooler (lower potential)

Patterns should reflect geographic and climatic variation

If the classification doesn't match your expectations:

Return to the Styling panel and adjust the colour ramp, number of classes, or classification mode

Click Apply again

Insert the Choropleth Map:

In the Items panel (right side), click Add Map

On the layout canvas, click and drag to draw a rectangle:

This rectangle defines the area where the map will appear

Release the mouse to place the map

Resize and reposition as needed by clicking and dragging corners/edges

The map should occupy about 60–70% of the layout

Add an Attribute Table to the Layout:

In the Items panel (right side), click Add Attribute Table

On the layout canvas, click and drag to draw a rectangle below or beside the map

Release to place the table
